exercise.name: Dumbbell Side Bend

reference.title: Dumbbell Side Bend
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Dumbbell, exercise type Strength

exercise.laterality: Unilateral load (one side at a time)

breathing.pattern: Inhale as you bend toward the dumbbell, exhale as you pull back up.
breathing.cadence: About 1.5 s down, short pause, about 1.5 s up

prescription.tempo: About 1.5 s down, brief pause, 1.5 s up
prescription.progression: Dumbbell load is user-chosen: pick a weight that leaves about 2-3 reps in reserve (RPE 7-8) at the end of each set. Many coaches prefer suitcase carries for the same muscles with less spine bending.

cues.text: Stand tall, feet hip width, dumbbell in the right hand at your side (palm facing the thigh), left fingertips lightly behind the head.
Breathe in and bend straight sideways toward the dumbbell; let it slide down the outside of the thigh.
Short pause at a comfortable stretch; no leaning forward or twisting.
Breathe out and pull the trunk back up with the opposite side of the waist, just past upright.
Stand tall; finish the set, then switch hands.

mistakes.mistake: Leaning forward or twisting as you bend
mistakes.fix: Move in a flat side plane, chest facing forward.

mistakes.mistake: Holding a dumbbell in each hand
mistakes.fix: One dumbbell only; two cancel each other out.

mistakes.mistake: Bending the arm or shrugging the dumbbell up
mistakes.fix: Arm long and relaxed; the waist does the work.

mistakes.mistake: Going too heavy and bouncing out of the bottom
mistakes.fix: Use a load you can lower in 1.5 s.

kinematics.norm: A comfortable side bend toward the weight and back to just past upright; no study fixes the range (clinical opinion)
Slides down the outside of the thigh, arm vertical (clinical opinion)
Square, with a small shift away from the bend (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #040712, Dumbbell Side Bend, video (movement reference)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
McGill, Juker and Kropf, quantitative intramuscular myoelectric activity of quadratus lumborum during a wide variety of tasks (Clinical Biomechanics)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Choose a dumbbell load you can control for every rep; the load is user-chosen.
Low-back pain with side bending: try a suitcase hold or carry (no bend) instead (clinical opinion).
Keep the range comfortable; repeated end-range bending under load is not needed.
modify: Free hand on the hip instead of behind the head.

muscleNotes.obliques_l: The obliques on the side opposite the dumbbell lower the trunk toward the weight under control and pull it back up; side-lying lateral flexion gave about 98% MVC external oblique in Konrad 2001 (no study measured the standing dumbbell version).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: Quadratus lumborum and the erector spinae opposite the load work with the obliques; quadratus lumborum is a primary lateral stabiliser of the spine (McGill, Juker and Kropf).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: The obliques on the dumbbell side finish the movement just past upright (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis and the deep abdominals keep the trunk from leaning forward or twisting (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.upper_traps_r: Keep the loaded shoulder from being pulled down (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_med_r: Keeps the pelvis level over the feet (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_med_l: Keeps the pelvis level over the feet (clinical opinion).
